questions.question: What happens to the bread and wine in the Eucharist, and how is Christ present?
shared_ground: 'This is my body' and 'this is my blood' quoted or affirmed (excludes memorial, decides nothing among the other four)
Christ's body and blood are truly given or received in the Supper (shared by spiritual presence, sacramental union, real change, transubstantiation)
Calling the Eucharist the body and blood of Christ, or the bread of life (all realist positions)
The Supper must be received worthily; unworthy eating brings judgment
The Supper is done in remembrance of Christ's death (all five positions)
Christ's body is in heaven at the Father's right hand (all positions affirm the ascension)

positions.name: Memorial

defined.quote: the mass is not a sacrifice, but is a remembrance of the sacrifice and assurance of the salvation which Christ has given us.

defined.source: Baptist Faith and Message, Article VII (2000)
defined.quote: The Lord's Supper is a symbolic act of obedience whereby members of the church, through partaking of the bread and the fruit of the vine, memorialize the death of the Redeemer and anticipate His second coming.

positions.statement: The bread and wine are symbols that call Christ's death to mind; Christ's body and blood are neither present in them nor received through them.
positions.mark: The passage says the bread and wine only represent or remind of Christ's body and blood, and that nothing more than this remembrance is given in the rite.
positions.first_defined: Zwingli, Sixty-Seven Articles (1523); Baptist Faith and Message (1925, revised 2000)

positions.name: Spiritual presence

defined.quote: the body and blood of Christ being then, not corporally or carnally, in, with, or under the bread and wine; yet, as really, but spiritually, present to the faith of believers in that ordinance
The Body of Christ is given, taken, and eaten, in the Supper, only after an heavenly and spiritual manner. And the mean whereby the Body of Christ is received and eaten in the Supper is Faith.
spiritually receive, and feed upon Christ crucified, and all the benefits of his death

positions.statement: Believers truly receive Christ's body and blood in the Supper, but spiritually and by faith; the body is not in or under the bread, and unbelievers receive only the outward signs.
positions.mark: The passage says Christ's body is received only spiritually or by faith (not by the mouth), or that unbelievers who eat receive the sign but not the body.
positions.first_defined: Consensus Tigurinus (1549); Thirty-Nine Articles (1563/1571); Westminster Confession (1646)

positions.name: Sacramental union

defined.quote: Of the Supper of the Lord they teach that the Body and Blood of Christ are truly present, and are distributed to those who eat the Supper of the Lord

defined.source: Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration VII.35 (1577)
defined.quote: under the bread, with the bread, in the bread [the body of Christ is present and offered], are employed, is that by means of them the papistical transubstantiation may be rejected and the sacramental union of the unchanged essence of the bread and of the body of Christ indicated

positions.statement: Christ's true body and blood are present in, with and under the bread and wine, which remain bread and wine in their essence, and are received by the mouth by all who eat, worthy or unworthy.
positions.mark: The passage says the bread remains bread (keeps its nature or substance) while Christ's true body is present with it or given with it.
positions.first_defined: Augsburg Confession, Article X (1530); Formula of Concord, Article VII (1577)

positions.name: Real change, manner undefined

defined.source: Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom, Epiclesis
defined.quote: And make this bread the precious Body of Your Christ. ... And that which is in this cup the precious Blood of Your Christ. ... Changing them by Your Holy Spirit.

defined.source: Longer Catechism of St Philaret of Moscow, q. 340 (1830s)
defined.quote: the word transubstantiation is not to be taken to define the manner in which the bread and wine are changed into the Body and Blood of the Lord; for this none can understand but God
It is by the conversion of the bread and wine into Christ's body and blood that Christ becomes present in this sacrament.

positions.statement: By God's action at the consecration the bread and wine are changed into, and become, Christ's body and blood, so that they are no longer simply bread and wine; how the change happens is not defined.
positions.mark: The passage says the bread and wine are changed, transformed or made into Christ's body and blood (a change in what they are), without saying how.
positions.first_defined: Prayed in the eastern epiclesis; stated by the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) and, for Catholics, Lateran IV (1215) and Trent (1551)

first_uncertain.author: Epiphanius of Salamis
first_uncertain.text: May this bread, having been transformed, become the body of Christ: a divine body, a body of salvation for souls and bodies. And that which has been mixed in this cup, the same blood of Christ—the blood of a new covenant—is a salvation to us, so that we all may partake in the mysteries of your saints in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.

memorial.quote: this bread, having been transformed, become the body of Christ
memorial.audited: ATTRIBUTION: the Greek 'Anaphora of Epiphanius' is of uncertain authorship and date; the 403 date is the bishop's, not the text's. 'May this bread, having been transformed, become the body of Christ' (Greek: ἄρτος οὗτος μετατραπεὶς γένηται σῶμα Χριστοῦ) says the bread becomes the body, not a mere reminder.

spiritual-presence.quote: May this bread, having been transformed, become the body of Christ
spiritual-presence.audited: ATTRIBUTION: the Greek 'Anaphora of Epiphanius' is of uncertain authorship and date; the 403 date is the bishop's, not the text's. The bread itself is to 'become the body of Christ' (μετατραπεὶς γένηται σῶμα Χριστοῦ), which rules out a body received only by faith and not in the bread.

sacramental-union.quote: May this bread, having been transformed, become the body of Christ
sacramental-union.audited: ATTRIBUTION: the Greek 'Anaphora of Epiphanius' is of uncertain authorship and date; the 403 date is the bishop's, not the text's. 'Having been transformed (μετατραπείς), become the body of Christ' says the bread is turned into the body, the opposite of the bread keeping its nature.

eucharistic-change.quote: this bread, having been transformed, become the body of Christ
eucharistic-change.audited: ATTRIBUTION: the Greek 'Anaphora of Epiphanius' is of uncertain authorship and date; the 403 date is the bishop's, not the text's. 'May this bread, having been transformed, become the body of Christ' is the change mark; the Greek μετατραπεὶς γένηται matches the English exactly. No manner is given.

first_uncertain.attribution_note: Authorship and date of this anaphora are uncertain.

positions.name: Transubstantiation

defined.quote: that wonderful and singular conversion of the whole substance of the bread into the Body, and of the whole substance of the wine into the Blood-the species Only of the bread and wine remaining-which conversion indeed the Catholic Church most aptly calls Transubstantiation
He be, in many other places, sacramentally present to us in his own substance, by a manner of existing, which, though we can scarcely express it in words

positions.statement: The whole substance of the bread and wine is converted into the substance of Christ's body and blood, while the appearances (everything the senses or any physical test can detect) remain; so the change is not physical or chemical.
positions.mark: The passage distinguishes what the bread is (now Christ's body) from what it still appears to be to the senses (bread), saying the appearance remains while the reality is changed.
positions.first_defined: Fourth Lateran Council (1215); Council of Trent, Session 13 (1551)

passages.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea
passages.text: Since the Spirit is the bread of the coming age, which is a food of life for the one approaching the age, and 'the bread which I will give' to you is 'my flesh for the life of the world' (John 6:51), and the blood is living in the body; and for this reason Moses said 'the life of all flesh' (Leviticus 17:11) regarding 'the blood' as being unified by blood. He clearly distinguished the type by the name of the truth, saying: 'this is my body'; and for this reason he named the types with the names of the truth, so that they would not be trivialized by what is seen, but would marvel at the power. Thus, eating and drinking showed the participation which would not have occurred without a body; for if the divine power had not been joined to a body and unified by blood, we would not have had communion through it to God.

memorial.quote: eating and drinking showed the participation which would not have occurred without a body; for if the divine power had not been joined to a body and unified by blood, we would not have had communion through it to God
memorial.audited: ATTRIBUTION: a catena fragment; the Greek opens 'τύπον δὲ ποιεῖ Ἀπολινάριος' ('Apollinaris makes [it] a type'), so a compiler is reporting him. It affirms 'this is my body' and says the types bear the names of the truth 'so that they would not be belittled for what is seen, but marvelled at for the power', which excludes a mere reminder. The English section omits the opening clause on 'participation in the body and blood accomplished in spirit for believers'.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.text: May this bread, having been transformed, become the body of Christ: a divine body, a body of salvation for souls and bodies. passages.author: Epiphanius of Salamis
passages.text: Having said to the apostles: Take, eat; this is my body, which is being broken for you for the forgiveness of sins. Likewise, after the supper, having taken a cup and mixing it from two elements, from the fruit of the vine and from water, he sealed the cup of immortality and gave it to his disciples, saying: Drink from it, all of you; this is my blood of the new covenant, which is being poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins.

memorial.quote: this is my body, which is being broken for you for the forgiveness of sins
memorial.audited: ATTRIBUTION: the Greek 'Anaphora of Epiphanius' is of uncertain authorship and date; the 403 date is the bishop's, not the text's. The anaphora recites 'Take, eat; this is my body' (τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ σῶμά μου) over the bread; the question's shared ground says this excludes memorial and decides nothing else.

passages.attribution_note: Authorship and date of this anaphora are uncertain.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: That Christ is life and life-giving. From the letter to the Corinthians: “I speak as to the wise; judge what I say. The cup of blessing that we bless — is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break — is it not a sharing in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we the many are one body; for we all partake of the one bread.” (1 Corinthians 10:15–17) Human flesh, as far as its own nature goes, would not be life-giving, nor would human blood if it were common and by itself; but Christ’s body and precious blood give life — and being able to give life belongs to God alone…

memorial.quote: The cup of blessing that we bless — is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break — is it not a sharing in the body of Christ?
memorial.audited: Cyril comments on 1 Cor 10 that 'Christ's body and precious blood give life', so the sharing is a real giving of the body, not a reminder only.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: The Lord gives thanks when he takes the cup — that is, in the form of prayer he converses with God the Father, declaring him as it were sharer and co-approver of the life-giving blessing that will be given to us, and at the same time giving us a pattern first to give thanks and thus to break the bread and distribute it. That is why we too, setting what was said before God’s face, beg intently that it be remolded for us into the spiritual blessing, so that by partaking of them we may be sanctified bodily and spiritually. He said demonstratively, “This is my body” (Matthew 26:26–28) and “This is my blood,” so that you may not think what appears is a mere type, but that through some ineffable energy of the God who can do all things what has been brought forward is truly changed into the body and blood of Christ — of which, when we partake, we take in Christ’s life-giving and sanctifying pow

memorial.quote: through some ineffable energy of the God who can do all things what has been brought forward is truly changed into the body and blood of Christ
memorial.audited: 'Truly changed into the body and blood of Christ' (μεταποιεῖσθαι εἰς σῶμα καὶ αἷμα Χριστοῦ κατὰ τὸ ἀληθές), and 'that you may not think what appears is a mere type', rule out a sign only.

spiritual-presence.quote: we take in Christ's life-giving and sanctifying power...mingled in us...through his holy flesh and precious blood
spiritual-presence.audited: What is set forth is 'truly changed into the body and blood of Christ' and is seen as 'flesh and blood lying before us on the holy tables', so the body is in what is received, not only by faith; the grader's quote was not the deciding line.

sacramental-union.quote: what has been brought forward is truly changed into the body and blood of Christ
sacramental-union.audited: 'What has been brought forward is truly changed (μεταποιεῖσθαι) into the body and blood' denies that the offerings stay what they were.

eucharistic-change.quote: what has been brought forward is truly changed into the body and blood of Christ
eucharistic-change.audited: 'Through some ineffable energy of God... what has been brought forward is truly changed into the body and blood of Christ'; the Greek μεταποιεῖσθαι... κατὰ τὸ ἀληθές is faithfully rendered, and 'ineffable' leaves the manner undefined.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: I myself receive by faith the flesh of the life-giving Word which gives life; therefore the Savior said, 'Those who eat from this bread will never taste death for eternity' (John 6:51); those who…

memorial.quote: I myself receive by faith the flesh of the life-giving Word which gives life
memorial.audited: ATTRIBUTION: the 'Dialogus cum Nestorio' is of doubtful authenticity as a work of Cyril. 'I myself receive by faith the flesh of the life-giving Word' (πίστει μεταλαμβάνω τὴν... ζωοποιοῦσαν σάρκα) says the flesh itself is received, which is more than a reminder.

passages.attribution_note: Widely doubted as Cyril's; some lines are given to Nestorius.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Since after the resurrection Christ was about to be taken up to the Father with a body, for this reason he has given us his own body and blood, so that his flesh and blood, dwelling in us, may make us holy and sharers of immortality (Matthew 26:26–28).

memorial.quote: he has given us his own body and blood, so that his flesh and blood, dwelling in us, may make us holy
memorial.audited: 'He has given us his own body and blood, so that his flesh and blood, dwelling in us, may make us holy' says the body is truly given, which excludes a sign only.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Cyril: That one who has become a sharer in Christ — by partaking of his holy flesh and blood — must also have his mind and love to go forward through inward achievements, understanding well what concerns him, he hinted at once by saying that head must be eaten with the feet and the inward parts. (Ex 12:9; Jn 6:53-56)

memorial.quote: by partaking of his holy flesh and blood
memorial.audited: 'One who has become a sharer in Christ by partaking of his holy flesh and blood' says the flesh and blood are truly partaken, more than a reminder.

questions.question: Is the Eucharist a sacrifice, and if so, of what kind?
shared_ground: Christ's sacrifice on the cross was once for all and complete (all positions affirm this)
The Supper remembers or proclaims Christ's death
Thanksgiving and praise are offered at the Eucharist (praise and propitiatory positions both affirm it)
Calling the Eucharist an 'offering' or 'sacrifice' with no statement of what is offered or for what purpose (decides between no-sacrifice and the others only)
Malachi 1:11 'pure offering' applied to Christian worship without further specification

positions.name: Not a sacrifice

defined.quote: the mass is not a sacrifice, but is a remembrance of the sacrifice and assurance of the salvation which Christ has given us.

positions.statement: The Supper is a remembrance of Christ's once-for-all sacrifice and is not itself a sacrifice in any sense.
positions.mark: The passage says the Supper is not a sacrifice at all, only a remembrance.
positions.first_defined: Zwingli, Sixty-Seven Articles (1523)

positions.name: Sacrifice of praise and commemoration only

defined.source: Apology of the Augsburg Confession, XXIV.19 (1531)
defined.quote: The other species is the eucharistic sacrifice, which does not merit the remission of sins or reconciliation, but is rendered by those who have been reconciled, in order that we may give thanks
In this sacrament, Christ is not offered up to his Father; nor any real sacrifice made at all, for remission of sins of the quick or dead; but only a commemoration of that one offering up of himself
Wherefore the sacrifices of Masses, in the which it was commonly said, that the Priest did offer Christ for the quick and the dead, to have remission of pain or guilt, were blasphemous fables

positions.statement: The Supper includes a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving and commemorates Christ's sacrifice, but Christ is not offered to God in it and it obtains no forgiveness for the living or the dead.
positions.mark: The passage limits the Eucharistic offering to praise, thanksgiving or remembrance, denying that Christ is offered or that it obtains forgiveness for anyone.
positions.first_defined: Augsburg Confession XXIV and Apology XXIV (1530-31); Thirty-Nine Articles XXXI (1563/71); Westminster 29.2 (1646)

positions.name: Propitiatory sacrifice

defined.quote: that same Christ is contained and immolated in an unbloody manner, who once offered Himself in a bloody manner on the altar of the cross

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 17 (1672)
defined.quote: it is a true and propitiatory Sacrifice offered for all Orthodox, living and dead
The sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice

positions.statement: In the Eucharist the one sacrifice of Christ is offered to God without bloodshed, and it obtains mercy and forgiveness for the living and the dead.
positions.mark: The passage says the Eucharist is offered for sins, or for the living and the dead to obtain mercy, or that Christ (his body and blood) is the victim offered in it.
positions.first_defined: Council of Trent, Session 22 (1562); Synod of Jerusalem (1672)

first_states.author: Cyril of Alexandria
first_states.text: Cyril: So then the matter is fruit-bearing, O Palladius, and a mystical word has also been woven for it, I think, carrying the riddle up unto Emmanuel, and unto us ourselves; and I will speak again as I am able. For when the holy and true tent has been shown in this world—that is, the Church—Christ conspicuous in it many-formedly and all but from us and for us is brought forward as a sacred victim to God and Father, a ransom and exchange of the life of all, one worth-all. And being one also himself, he was being written according to many manners, as at least in the bringing-for

no-sacrifice.quote: Christ conspicuous in it many-formedly and all but from us and for us is brought forward as a sacred victim to God and Father
no-sacrifice.audited: Kept. 'Christ will be brought forward toward us and for us, being sacrificed mystically in the holy tents' (Greek μυστικῶς ἱερουργούμενος ἐν ταῖς ἁγίαις σκηναῖς), with a daily offering in the Church.

sacrifice-of-praise.quote: brought forward as a sacred victim to God and Father, a ransom and exchange of the life of all
sacrifice-of-praise.audited: Kept. In the Church 'Christ ... from us and for us is brought forward as a sacred victim to God and Father' (Greek ὡς ἱερὸν προσάγεται θύμα τῷ Θεῷ καὶ Πατρί), so Christ himself is offered.

propitiatory-sacrifice.quote: Christ ... is brought forward as a sacred victim to God and Father, a ransom and exchange of the life of all
propitiatory-sacrifice.audited: Kept. Christ is named as the victim offered in the churches, 'from us and for us ... a sacred victim to God and Father, a ransom and exchange of the life of all', and 'being sacrificed mystically in the holy tents' daily; Greek checked and faithful (ὡς ἱερὸν προσάγεται θύμα; μυστικῶς ἱερουργούμενος). Note the first clause carries Cyril's hedge μονονουχί ('all but'); the later clause does not.

passages.author: Origen of Alexandria
passages.text: With God permitting, then, and secondly the bishops, and thirdly the presbyters and the people too, I will speak again of what is stirring me at this point. The offering is always made to God Almighty through Jesus Christ, as offering his divinity to the Father. Let the offering not be made twice, but to God through God.

no-sacrifice.quote: The offering is always made to God Almighty through Jesus Christ, as offering his divinity to the Father.
no-sacrifice.audited: Kept. In a liturgical setting (bishops, presbyters, people) Origen says 'the offering is always made to God Almighty through Jesus Christ' (Greek Ἀεὶ προσφορὰ γίνεται Θεῷ παντοκράτορι διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ), calling the eucharistic prosphora an offering to God; the English is faithful. The year given is Origen's death; the Dialogue dates c. 245.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Cyril: …for we approach the holy things, for no other grace, than so as to share the holy Christ through the unspeakable and spiritual sacrifice. And the vessels serving the sacrifices are also thoroughly cleansed, so that they may not become for some other, nor may the things having liturgized for the sacred be carried under to humans’ needs. And the law has been kept, and is saved in churches. And that being blessed is fitting for those playing-the-man, the law will clarify again saying: ‘Every male among the priests will eat them.’ (Leviticus 6:30)

questions.question: What authority does the bishop of Rome hold over the whole Church?
shared_ground: Peter was a leading apostle, named first in the lists
Peter and Paul taught and died in Rome; Rome is an apostolic church
Rome is an important church whose faith is praised
Communion between churches, including with Rome, matters
Bishops succeed the apostles in their sees

positions.name: No special authority

defined.source: Treatise on the Power and Primacy of the Pope, 9 (1537)
defined.quote: Christ sends forth His disciples on an equality, without any distinction
The Bishop of Rome hath no jurisdiction in this Realm of England
neither can the Pope of Rome in any sense be head thereof

positions.statement: The bishop of Rome holds no authority or rank over other churches by divine institution; all ministers are equal.
positions.mark: The passage says the apostles or bishops are all equal and that none, including Rome's, holds a God-given rank or authority over others.
positions.first_defined: Treatise on the Power and Primacy of the Pope (1537); Thirty-Nine Articles (1563/1571)

positions.name: Primacy of honour among equals

defined.source: Moscow Patriarchate, Position on the problem of primacy in the Universal Church (2013)
defined.quote: In the first millennium of church history, the primacy of honour used to belong to the chair of Rome.

defined.source: Moscow Patriarchate, Position on the problem of primacy in the Universal Church (2013)
defined.quote: They also believed that primacy in honour accorded to the bishops of Rome is instituted not by God but men.

positions.statement: Rome held first place in honour among the churches, granted by the Church and not by divine right, without jurisdiction over other local churches.
positions.mark: The passage gives Rome first rank or precedence while denying it jurisdiction over other churches, or grounds its rank in councils or the city rather than in Christ's grant to Peter.
positions.first_defined: Councils of Constantinople (381, canon 3) and Chalcedon (451, canon 28) on the order of sees; Moscow Patriarchate statement (2013)

positions.name: Primacy of jurisdiction by divine right

defined.source: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 2 (1870)
defined.quote: Therefore whoever succeeds to the chair of Peter obtains by the institution of Christ himself, the primacy of Peter over the whole church.
to him was committed in blessed Peter the full power of tending, ruling and governing the whole church

positions.statement: By Christ's institution, the bishop of Rome as Peter's successor holds full and immediate power to govern the whole Church.
positions.mark: The passage says Rome's bishop, as Peter's successor, has authority (not only honour) over all churches, such as to judge, depose or bind other bishops, by Christ's grant.
positions.first_defined: Council of Florence (1439); First Vatican Council (1870)

positions.name: Infallibility of solemn papal definitions

defined.source: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4 (1870)
defined.quote: when the Roman pontiff speaks EX CATHEDRA, that is, when, in the exercise of his office as shepherd and teacher of all Christians, in virtue of his supreme apostolic authority, he defines a doctrine concerning faith or morals to be held by the whole church, he possesses ... that infallibility which the divine Redeemer willed his church to enjoy

defined.source: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4 (1870)
defined.quote: such definitions of the Roman pontiff are of themselves, and not by the consent of the church, irreformable.

positions.statement: When the bishop of Rome solemnly defines a doctrine of faith or morals for the whole Church, he cannot err, and the definition binds without the Church's later consent.
positions.mark: The passage says a Roman bishop's doctrinal decision cannot be in error, or is final in itself without needing a council's or the churches' acceptance.
positions.first_defined: First Vatican Council, Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4 (1870)

questions.question: May Mary be called Mother of God (Theotokos)?
shared_ground: Mary is the mother of Jesus
Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit of the virgin Mary
Mary did not give the Word his divine nature

positions.name: Mother of God (Theotokos)

defined.source: Council of Ephesus, Cyril's First Anathema (431)
defined.quote: If anyone does not confess that Emmanuel is God in truth, and therefore that the holy virgin is the mother of God

defined.source: Council of Chalcedon, Definition of Faith (451)
defined.quote: in the last days the same for us and for our salvation from Mary, the virgin God-bearer as regards his humanity

positions.statement: Because the one born of Mary is God the Word made flesh, Mary is rightly called Mother of God.
positions.mark: The passage calls Mary Mother of God or God-bearer, or says God was born of her.
positions.first_defined: Council of Ephesus (431); Council of Chalcedon (451)

first_states.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea (quoted as Athanasius)
first_states.text: So the one born from the holy virgin is Son of God by nature and true God, not by grace and sharing. Only according to the flesh from Mary is he human; according to the Spirit he himself is Son of God and God.

positions.statement: Mary should be called mother of Christ, not Mother of God, because she bore the humanity, not the Godhead.
positions.mark: The passage refuses the title Mother of God, preferring mother of Christ or of the man.
positions.first_defined: Condemned at Ephesus (431)

first_uncertain.author: Nestorius (as quoted)
first_uncertain.text: Nestorius says: When the divine Scripture speaks of the birth of Christ from Mary the virgin, it nowhere appears as God, but as Christ or the Lord Jesus, because these three terms are significant of the two natures, now referring to one, now to the other; I mean: When the birth from the Virgin is announced to us of Christ, the Apostle says, 'God sent his Son, born of a woman'; he did not say, 'Sent God the Word'; but he takes the name indicating the two births, namely God and man, because Christ is double; for the Virgin bore a Son of God, as he breathed; but you are gods and sons of the Most High all, whence we learned to say Christotokos, Kyriotokos, anthropotokos from Scripture, but we were never taught to call the holy virgin Theotokos, that is, God-bearer or Mother of God.

theotokos.quote: we were never taught to call the holy virgin Theotokos, that is, God-bearer or Mother of God
theotokos.audited: Nestorius's words: 'we were never taught to call the holy virgin Theotokos'. Greek confirmed: 'Θεοτόκον δὲ οὐδαμῶς ἐδιδάχθημεν λέγειν τὴν ἁγίαν Παρθένον'. ATTRIBUTION: these are Nestorius's words, not Cyril's, and the Dialogue with Nestorius is widely treated as not by Cyril; credit them to Nestorius (c. 428-431).

christotokos.quote: we learned to say Christotokos, Kyriotokos, anthropotokos from Scripture, but we were never taught to call the holy virgin Theotokos, that is, God-bearer or Mother of God
christotokos.audited: 'we learned to say Christotokos, Kyriotokos, anthropotokos ... but never ... Theotokos' (Χριστοτόκον ... Θεοτόκον δὲ οὐδαμῶς) is the mark: it refuses Mother of God and prefers mother of Christ. ATTRIBUTION: the speaker is Nestorius; the dialogue's ascription to Cyril is doubtful.

first_uncertain.attribution_note: Nestorius' words, quoted in a dialogue whose ascription to Cyril is doubted.

passages.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea (quoted as Athanasius)
passages.text: — worshiped, and worshiped with his flesh in one worship. Not two sons: one a true Son of God who is worshiped, and another a human from Mary who is not worshiped, made a son of God by grace as humans are. But the one from God, as I said — one Son of God and God, himself and no other — also born from Mary according to the flesh in the last days, as the angel said to the God-bearer Mary when she asked, “How will this be, since I do not know a man?” — “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who is born will be called Son of God.” (Luke 1:34–35)

theotokos.quote: as the angel said to the God-bearer Mary
theotokos.audited: 'as the angel said to the God-bearer Mary'; Greek 'τῇ θεοτόκῳ Μαρίᾳ' confirmed. passages.author: Amphilochius of Iconium
passages.text: O Mary, O Mary, who has possessed the firstborn Creator of all things! O humanity, who has made the eternal Word of God bodily present and has been honored in this place by the heavenly and noetic powers! For Christ was not worthy to be formed into the likenesses of the archangels, nor even into the unchangeable images of the principalities, powers, and authorities, but into you, who were drawn into a turn and associated with irrational animals. For those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but she who is seized by frequent and such a disease has found a physician such that it is a greater happiness of health to have escaped the sickness. But where now is the hostile and senseless, the wandering and riotous dragon, promising to lift his own throne to the height? Therefore, brothers, called to the participation in the heavenly calling of blessedness, called to the adoption of God

theotokos.quote: O Mary, who has possessed the firstborn Creator of all things! O humanity, who has made the eternal Word of God bodily present
theotokos.audited: 'O Mary, who has possessed the firstborn Creator of all things'. The Greek (ἡ τὸν τῶν ἁπάντων δημιουργὸν πρωτότοκον κεκτημένη) means she has the Creator of all as her firstborn son, so God was born of her. The English 'the firstborn Creator' undersells this; the original is stronger.

christotokos.quote: O Mary, who has possessed the firstborn Creator of all things! O humanity, who has made the eternal Word of God bodily present
christotokos.audited: Saying Mary has 'the Creator of all things' as her firstborn (τὸν τῶν ἁπάντων δημιουργὸν πρωτότοκον) says God was born of her, which rules out mother-of-Christ-only.

passages.author: Didymus the Blind
passages.text: 27.17 But Isaiah cries out to Him without comparison as the God the Father: 'From eternity we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen a God besides You' (Isa 64:4). 27.18 For we saw no other God than the one born according to the saving incarnation from the Virgin Mary, nor did we hear [of any] except the one attested by God the Father: 27.19 'This is my beloved Son' (Matt 3:17).

theotokos.quote: we saw no other God than the one born according to the saving incarnation from the Virgin Mary
theotokos.audited: 'we saw no other God than the one born ... from the Virgin Mary'; Greek 'θεὸν ἢ τὸν ἐκ παρθένου Μαρίας ... τεχθέντα' confirmed. God was born of her. ATTRIBUTION: De Trinitate's ascription to Didymus is disputed by modern scholars; treat the 398 date as doubtful.

christotokos.quote: we saw no other God than the one born according to the saving incarnation from the Virgin Mary
christotokos.audited: 'no other God than the one born ... from the Virgin Mary' (θεὸν ... ἐκ παρθένου Μαρίας ... τεχθέντα) says God was born of her. ATTRIBUTION: De Trinitate's ascription to Didymus is disputed.

passages.attribution_note: Attribution of De Trinitate to Didymus is disputed.

passages.author: John Chrysostom (quoted by Cyril)
passages.text: From John, bishop of Constantinople, on the divine birth. He says of the holy virgin: “Instead of a sun, he says, she contains without limit the sun of righteousness. Nature’s order is overcome; for he willed, he was able, he came down, he saved — all things run together for God. Today the One who is is born, and the One who is becomes what he was not. Being God, he becomes human without leaving off being God. He did not become human by departing from deity, nor become God by climbing up from humanity. Being Word, he became flesh without suffering change; his nature remained unchanged.” (Malachi 4:2) He adds: “He who sits on a high and lifted throne is laid in a manger. The untouchable, simple, bodiless one is wrapped by human hands. He who breaks the bonds of sin is tangled in swaddling cloths.” (Isaiah 6:1)

christotokos.quote: Being God, he becomes human without leaving off being God. He did not become human by departing from deity
christotokos.audited: Borderline but met: said 'of the holy virgin', 'Today the One who is is born ... Being God, he becomes human' says God was born of her. ATTRIBUTION: Cyril quotes these as John Chrysostom 'on the divine birth'; they are not Cyril's words, and the Chrysostom ascription should be checked.

passages.attribution_note: Quoted by Cyril as Chrysostom; the ascription still needs checking.

passages.author: Antiochus of Ptolemais (quoted by Cyril)
passages.text: From bishop Antiochus: “For yesterday, in undefiled birth pangs, the life-bearer, the fair-bearer, the great-bearer, the light-bearer, the hope-bearer, the God-bearer, the strange-bearer, the virgin-mother Mary brought us a Savior.” (John 1:14)

theotokos.quote: the God-bearer, the virgin-mother Mary brought us a Savior
theotokos.audited: 'the God-bearer ... Mary'; Greek 'ἡ θεοτόκος' confirmed in the list of titles. ATTRIBUTION: these are Antiochus of Ptolemais's words (d. c. 408) quoted by Cyril, not Cyril's own.

christotokos.quote: the God-bearer, the virgin-mother Mary brought us a Savior
christotokos.audited: Calls Mary 'the God-bearer' (ἡ θεοτόκος), which excludes mother-of-Christ-only. Words are Antiochus of Ptolemais's, quoted by Cyril.

passages.author: Severian of Gabala (quoted by Cyril)
passages.text: From bishop Severianus: “For the Word begotten from above from the Father — beyond speech, beyond telling, beyond grasp, eternally — is himself begotten in time from below from the virgin Mary, so that those first born from below may be born from above from a second birth, that is, from God.” (John 3:3–7)

theotokos.quote: the Word ... is himself begotten in time ... from the virgin Mary
theotokos.audited: 'the Word begotten from above from the Father ... is himself begotten in time from below from the virgin Mary': the Word is born of her. Greek 'ὁ αὐτὸς ἐν χρόνῳ γεννᾶται κάτωθεν ἐκ παρθένου Μαρίας' confirmed. ATTRIBUTION: Severian of Gabala's words (d. after 408), quoted by Cyril.

christotokos.quote: the Word ... is himself begotten in time ... from the virgin Mary
christotokos.audited: 'the Word ... is himself (ὁ αὐτός) begotten in time ... from the virgin Mary' says God the Word was born of her. Words are Severian of Gabala's, quoted by Cyril.

passages.author: Ammonius of Adrianople (quoted by Cyril)
passages.text: From Ammonius, bishop of Adrianople: “For he too said somewhere about the Word of God: But if he himself is God by nature, as God’s Only-begotten Son, and in taking the slave’s form was also counted worthy to be called firstborn son of the holy virgin, he gave himself as a ransom for all.” He goes on: “I have already shown the impiety into which the Arians fall when they say the God-bearer Mary needed the sacrifices then offered under the law for women who give birth.”

theotokos.audited: 'the God-bearer Mary'; Greek 'τὴν θεοτόκον Μαρίαν' confirmed. ATTRIBUTION: Ammonius of Adrianople's words, quoted by Cyril, not Cyril's own.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: This statement shows the manifest confession, namely the exaltation, and the phrase 'You are my Son' establishes His eternal nature, while the phrase 'I have today begotten you' reveals His birth according to the flesh, which He willingly underwent through the Holy Virgin, and by which He is also named Theotokos.

theotokos.quote: by which He is also named Theotokos
theotokos.audited: 'by which He is also named Theotokos'. TRANSLATION: the Greek is 'ταύτῃ τοι καὶ θεότοκος ὠνόμασται', meaning the holy Virgin, through whom he was born in the flesh, is for this reason named Theotokos. 'He' is wrong; it should be 'she'. ATTRIBUTION: catena fragment; same text as the Psalm fragment b0c5e1ecd5244d19.

christotokos.quote: by which He is also named Theotokos
christotokos.audited: Greek 'ταύτῃ τοι καὶ θεότοκος ὠνόμασται' names the Virgin Theotokos, which excludes mother-of-Christ-only. The English 'He is named' is a mistranslation.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: You see the confession at the very start, that is, the declaration. For the Father has set down the words "You are" in order to show the Son's eternal being. He did not become Son in time; he always was this—that is, Son. Then the Father brought in the words "Today I have begotten you" (Psalm 2:7) in order to show his recent birth according to the flesh, which he willingly underwent through the holy Virgin. This is why she has been named Mother of God. For she gave birth not to a mere human being simply joined to God by a mere external union, but rather to the very Word from God the Father, who put on human lowliness and became a human being like us.

theotokos.quote: This is why she has been named Mother of God. For she gave birth not to a mere human being simply joined to God by a mere external union, but rather to the very Word from God the Father, who put on human lowliness and became a human being like us.
theotokos.audited: 'This is why she has been named Mother of God. For she gave birth not to a mere human being ... but rather to the very Word'. A direct statement of the mark.

christotokos.quote: she gave birth not to a mere human being simply joined to God by a mere external union, but rather to the very Word from God the Father, who put on human lowliness and became a human being like us.
christotokos.audited: 'she gave birth not to a mere human being simply joined to God ... but rather to the very Word' rejects the excluding claim word for word.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: From Luke. “And it came to pass while they were there that the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she bore her son, the firstborn, and wrapped him and laid him in the manger, because there was no place for them in the lodging.” (Luke 2:6–7) The holy virgin has borne one and only son, Emmanuel. How then does it say “her son, the firstborn” (Romans 8:29)? For others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin. So it is marked from the God-breathed scripture: the Only-begotten Word of God has been named firstborn. For he has shared blood and flesh and similarly to us shared the same things. Thus he became firstborn among many brothers; yet as God he is worshiped by us ourselves and by the spirits above.

theotokos.quote: the holy virgin has borne ... the Only-begotten Word of God has been named firstborn
theotokos.audited: Borderline but met: 'The holy virgin has borne one and only son, Emmanuel ... the Only-begotten Word of God has been named firstborn' identifies her firstborn son with the Only-begotten Word, so the Word was born of her. Greek 'μόνον τέτοκεν υἱὸν τὸν Ἐμμανουὴλ ἡ ἁγία παρθένος' confirmed.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: If the church belongs to God and Christ has presented it to himself, then it is clear that God is the one who has come from the holy and God-bearing Mary.

theotokos.quote: God is the one who has come from the holy and God-bearing Mary
theotokos.audited: 'God is the one who has come from the holy and God-bearing Mary': calls her God-bearing and says God came from her.

christotokos.quote: God is the one who has come from the holy and God-bearing Mary
christotokos.audited: 'God is the one who has come from the holy and God-bearing Mary' says God was born of her.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: We say that this same Only-begotten Word, begotten beyond speech from the substance of God the Father, maker of the ages, the one through whom and in whom all things are, the true light, the nature that gives life to all — for he has appeared as life from the Father’s life — in the last times of the age, when the Father was pleased to save the race on earth that had fallen under a curse and been brought down by sin into death and decay, took hold of Abraham’s seed, as the Scriptures say, shared blood and flesh — that is, became human — and taking flesh and making it his own, was born in the flesh through the holy God-bearer Mary (Hebrews 2:16).

theotokos.quote: was born in the flesh through the holy God-bearer Mary
theotokos.audited: 'was born in the flesh through the holy God-bearer Mary'; Greek 'διὰ τῆς ἁγίας καὶ θεοτόκου Μαρίας' confirmed.

christotokos.quote: was born in the flesh through the holy God-bearer Mary
christotokos.audited: 'the holy God-bearer Mary' (θεοτόκου Μαρίας) uses the title the position refuses.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: But the word God-bearer was already customary even with the holy fathers before us, who are admired for right faith, and still with all under heaven, so to speak. I thought I had to declare that as true.

theotokos.quote: the word God-bearer was already customary even with the holy fathers before us
theotokos.audited: 'the word God-bearer was already customary even with the holy fathers ... I thought I had to declare that as true': Cyril affirms the title.

christotokos.quote: I thought I had to declare that as true
christotokos.audited: Affirming 'the word God-bearer' as true and customary rules out refusing it.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: But we do say this: look — all the best and wisest fathers of our times also name the holy virgin God-bearer, and they affirm that the Word from God has been united by nature to the flesh, that he came to be in the virgin’s womb, and that he came forth from her according to the flesh.

theotokos.quote: all the best and wisest fathers of our times also name the holy virgin God-bearer
theotokos.audited: 'all the best and wisest fathers of our times also name the holy virgin God-bearer'; Greek 'θεοτόκον ὀνομάζουσι τὴν ἁγίαν παρθένον' confirmed.

christotokos.quote: all the best and wisest fathers of our times also name the holy virgin God-bearer
christotokos.audited: Endorses naming the virgin 'God-bearer' (θεοτόκον), the title the position refuses.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: For the Son from God the Father by nature, taking to himself an ensouled and intelligent body, has been begotten according to the flesh through the holy virgin and Theotokos Mary — not turned into flesh (far from it!), but rather taking it on, and not neglecting to be God.

theotokos.quote: through the holy virgin and Theotokos Mary
theotokos.audited: 'begotten according to the flesh through the holy virgin and Theotokos Mary'; Greek 'διὰ τῆς ἁγίας παρθένου καὶ θεοτόκου Μαρίας' confirmed.

christotokos.quote: through the holy virgin and Theotokos Mary
christotokos.audited: Uses 'Theotokos' (θεοτόκου Μαρίας) as her title.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: — not a mere human begotten from her, but the Word himself enfleshed, with a body from her as his own. That is why he is said to have been begotten in the flesh: he makes the begetting of his own flesh his.

theotokos.quote: not a mere human begotten from her, but the Word himself enfleshed, with a body from her as his own
theotokos.audited: 'not a mere human begotten from her, but the Word himself enfleshed ... he is said to have been begotten in the flesh': the Word was born of her.

christotokos.quote: not a mere human begotten from her, but the Word himself enfleshed
christotokos.audited: 'not a mere human begotten from her, but the Word himself' rejects 'she bore only a man' directly.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Those who senselessly deny that the holy virgin is God-bearer are forced to say there are two sons of God. For if she did not bear in the flesh the enfleshed God, they must admit — willing or not — that she bore only a common human, with nothing more than we have.

theotokos.quote: Those who senselessly deny that the holy virgin is God-bearer are forced to say there are two sons of God
theotokos.audited: 'Those who senselessly deny that the holy virgin is God-bearer'; Greek 'θεοτόκον οὐκ εἶναι τὴν ἁγίαν παρθένον' confirmed.

christotokos.quote: Those who senselessly deny that the holy virgin is God-bearer
christotokos.audited: Condemns those who 'deny that the holy virgin is God-bearer', which is the christotokos position itself.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: So if they say that the one born from the holy virgin is true God — that is, the Word from God the Father united by nature to flesh — why do they fear to confess that the holy virgin is God-bearer?

theotokos.quote: why do they fear to confess that the holy virgin is God-bearer?
theotokos.audited: 'why do they fear to confess that the holy virgin is God-bearer?': urges the title outright.

christotokos.quote: why do they fear to confess that the holy virgin is God-bearer?
christotokos.audited: Rebukes those who 'fear to confess that the holy virgin is God-bearer'.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: In the same breath he sets down two things proper to God, and not fitting for human nature. Of the one born from Mary he said that those saved through him are his own people, and that he himself will also free them from sins. All things belong to God, and to him alone it would befit to be able to free sinners from sins. So the one begotten from the holy virgin is God, whose own people we are; and he has freed us from sins, as one who has authority for that too.

theotokos.quote: So the one begotten from the holy virgin is God, whose own people we are
theotokos.audited: 'So the one begotten from the holy virgin is God': God was born of her.

christotokos.quote: So the one begotten from the holy virgin is God, whose own people we are
christotokos.audited: 'the one begotten from the holy virgin is God' says God was born of her.

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: Since he emptied himself by becoming in the likeness of a man, and was found in the form of a man, he receives the common name, that is, Christ and Jesus, or rather, Emmanuel. The name Emmanuel signifies 'God with us.' For it is written, 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel' (Isaiah 7:14). For the blessed Gabriel revealed the mystery to the holy and God-bearing virgin, saying, 'Do not fear, Mary, for you have found favor with God, and behold, you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he shall save his people from their sins' (Matthew 1:21-23). Are the prophet and the blessed angel inconsistent with one another? Not at all. For the blessed prophet speaks mysteries by the Spirit, having foretold a God who has become with us, naming him so both from his nature and from the economy of the flesh.

theotokos.quote: the holy and God-bearing virgin
theotokos.audited: 'the holy and God-bearing virgin': Cyril calls her God-bearer.

passages.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
passages.text: However, just as we have heard of the woman's transgressions, we must also learn of her achievements, for the Theotokos introduced virginity to life, carried God in her womb, and gave birth to Him in the flesh, renewing our race.

theotokos.quote: the Theotokos introduced virginity to life, carried God in her womb, and gave birth to Him in the flesh
theotokos.audited: 'the Theotokos ... carried God in her womb, and gave birth to Him in the flesh'. Both title and claim are stated.

christotokos.quote: the Theotokos introduced virginity to life, carried God in her womb, and gave birth to Him in the flesh
christotokos.audited: 'carried God in her womb, and gave birth to Him in the flesh' says God was born of her.

passages.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
passages.text: Therefore, even that which is being born shall be called the holy Son of God. Do you see how immense the dignity of the Mother of God is, being a virgin.

theotokos.quote: Do you see how immense the dignity of the Mother of God is, being a virgin.
theotokos.audited: 'Do you see how immense the dignity of the Mother of God is'; Greek 'τὸ τῆς θεοτόκου παρθένου ... ἀξίωμα' confirmed.

christotokos.quote: Do you see how immense the dignity of the Mother of God is, being a virgin.
christotokos.audited: Calls her the Theotokos virgin (τῆς θεοτόκου παρθένου).

questions.question: Did Mary remain a virgin all her life?
shared_ground: Mary conceived Jesus as a virgin (virginal conception)
Mary is called 'the Virgin' as a title in connection with Christ's birth

positions.name: Perpetual virginity

defined.quote: The deepening of faith in the virginal motherhood led the Church to confess Mary's real and perpetual virginity even in the act of giving birth to the Son of God made man.

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 7 (1672)
defined.quote: being conceived of the Holy Spirit, in the womb of the ever-virgin Mary

defined.source: Kontakion of the Dormition (Orthodox Church in America)
defined.quote: she was translated into life by Him who dwelt in her ever-virginal womb.

positions.statement: Mary remained a virgin before, in and after Jesus' birth, and had no other children.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary stayed a virgin after Jesus' birth, or calls her ever-virgin, or says the Lord's brothers were not her children.
positions.first_defined: 'Ever-virgin' at the Second Council of Constantinople (553); Lateran Synod (649)

first_states.author: Cyril of Alexandria
first_states.text: From Luke. “And it came to pass while they were there that the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she bore her son, the firstborn, and wrapped him and laid him in the manger, because there was no place for them in the lodging.” (Luke 2:6–7) The holy virgin has borne one and only son, Emmanuel. How then does it say “her son, the firstborn” (Romans 8:29)? For others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin. So it is marked from the God-breathed scripture: the Only-begotten Word of God has been named firstborn. For he has shared blood and flesh and similarly to us shared the same things. Thus he became firstborn among many brothers; yet as God he is worshiped by us ourselves and by the spirits above.

ever-virgin.quote: For others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin.
ever-virgin.audited: 'For others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin' (Greek οὐ γὰρ γεγόνασιν ἕτεροι μετ' αὐτόν, μεμένηκε δὲ παρθένος; checked, faithful): no other children and virginity after the birth.

other-children.quote: For others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin.
other-children.audited: 'Others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin' denies other children of Mary.

positions.name: Mary had other children
positions.statement: After Jesus' birth Mary and Joseph lived as married and had other children, the Lord's brothers and sisters.
positions.mark: The passage says the Lord's brothers were Mary's own sons, or that she did not remain a virgin after Jesus' birth.
positions.first_defined: No confession defines it

passages.author: Cyril of Alexandria
passages.text: From Luke. “And it came to pass while they were there that the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she bore her son, the firstborn, and wrapped him and laid him in the manger, because there was no place for them in the lodging.” (Luke 2:6–7) The holy virgin has borne one and only son, Emmanuel. How then does it say “her son, the firstborn” (Romans 8:29)? For others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin. So it is marked from the God-breathed scripture: the Only-begotten Word of God has been named firstborn. For he has shared blood and flesh and similarly to us shared the same things. Thus he became firstborn among many brothers; yet as God he is worshiped by us ourselves and by the spirits above.

ever-virgin.quote: For others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin.
ever-virgin.audited: 'For others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin' (Greek οὐ γὰρ γεγόνασιν ἕτεροι μετ' αὐτόν, μεμένηκε δὲ παρθένος; checked, faithful): no other children and virginity after the birth.

other-children.quote: For others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin.
other-children.audited: 'Others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin' denies other children of Mary.

passages.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
passages.text: The Virgin Mary kept her breasts untouched and nursed a child without knowing the child's father. She became a mother without becoming a bride, a remarkable and unprecedented event. A son was being raised, and yet, a father was not found. The field was bearing fruit, but the fruit had no farmer to tend to it. The beast gave birth, but it did not receive seed. A river was flowing, and its source was closed from everywhere, signifying that Mary had become a mother without suffering the things that mothers normally experience. She gave birth like a woman, but she was not corrupted like a woman. Her pregnancy was according to the law of nature, as she waited for the appointed time of childbirth. However, her conception was contrary to the law of nature. You introduced the king, with the doors closed, but again you led him out. For neither when he was being conceived nor when he was being bor

ever-virgin.quote: The Virgin Mary kept her breasts untouched and nursed a child without knowing the child's father. She became a mother without becoming a bride... For neither when he was being conceived nor when he was being born did the king of glory open the doors of your womb or loosen the bonds of your virginity.
ever-virgin.audited: The sealed fountain is glossed as 'no marital branch' drawing from her spring (Greek κλάδος γαμικὸς τὴν σὴν ...), i.e. no married union. Borderline: most of the passage is virginity in birth, and English 'you have remained untouched' adds 'remained' to the aorist οὐχ ἥψατο.

other-children.quote: For neither when he was being conceived nor when he was being born did the king of glory open the doors of your womb or loosen the bonds of your virginity. The bridegroom has called you 'a garden enclosed' and 'a fountain sealed', for you have remained untouched by the forces of corruption and decay.
other-children.audited: The sealed fountain from which no marital use drew rules out Mary bearing children to Joseph. Borderline for the same reason as ever-virgin.

questions.question: Was Mary free from sin, and from when?
shared_ground: Mary is holy, blessed, highly favoured
Mary as the new Eve, obedient where Eve disobeyed
Mary needed and received God's grace

positions.name: Mary had personal faults
positions.statement: Mary, though holy, committed some personal faults, such as doubt or vanity, like other believers.
positions.mark: The passage attributes a sin, fault, doubt or weakness to Mary.
positions.first_defined: No confession defines it

positions.name: Free from personal sin

defined.quote: except by a special privilege from God, as the Church holds in regard of the Blessed Virgin

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 6 (1672)
defined.quote: and especially the Mother of God the Word, the ever-virgin Mary, did not experience these [sins], or such like faults.

positions.statement: Mary never committed any personal sin during her life, by a special grace of God.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary committed no sin, or was wholly pure in her life, without saying anything about her conception.
positions.first_defined: Council of Trent, Session 6, Canon 23 (1547); Synod of Jerusalem, Decree 6 (1672)

positions.name: Immaculate Conception

defined.quote: the most Blessed Virgin Mary, in the first instance of her conception, by a singular grace and privilege granted by Almighty God, in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Savior of the human race, was preserved free from all stain of original sin

positions.statement: From the first moment of her conception Mary was preserved from original sin, by a grace given in view of Christ's merits.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary was without original sin, or holy from her conception, not only free from personal sin.
positions.first_defined: Pius IX, Ineffabilis Deus (1854)

questions.question: How did Mary's earthly life end?
shared_ground: Mary's earthly life came to an end
Mary is honoured in heaven
Mary's 'falling asleep' named without saying what happened to her body (fits all three)

positions.name: Died and was buried; nothing further held
positions.statement: Mary died and was buried like other believers, and awaits the general resurrection.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary's body lies in the grave or awaits the general resurrection, or that her end is unknown.
positions.first_defined: No confession defines it

positions.name: Died, then taken bodily to heaven (Dormition)

defined.source: Troparion and Kontakion of the Dormition (Orthodox Church in America)
defined.quote: in falling asleep you did not forsake the world, O Theotokos.

defined.source: Kontakion of the Dormition (Orthodox Church in America)
defined.quote: Neither the tomb, nor death had power over the Theotokos

positions.statement: Mary truly died (fell asleep), and was then raised and taken into heavenly life; neither tomb nor death held her.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary died and that afterwards her body did not remain in the tomb, or that she was raised.
positions.first_defined: Liturgical feast of the Dormition (from the 6th century); not defined as dogma

positions.name: Assumed body and soul (Catholic dogma)

defined.quote: that the Immaculate Mother of God, the ever Virgin Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory.

positions.statement: At the end of her earthly life Mary was taken body and soul into heavenly glory; the dogma leaves open whether she first died.
positions.mark: The passage says Mary was taken body and soul into heaven.
positions.first_defined: Pius XII, Munificentissimus Deus (1950)

questions.question: What is the relationship between Christians on earth and the saints in heaven?
shared_ground: The saints are honoured and remembered as examples of faith (Augsburg XXI: 'the memory of saints may be set before us')
Living Christians should pray for one another
Christ is the one mediator between God and humanity
Feasts or remembrance of martyrs on their days

positions.name: Remembered as examples only

defined.quote: Religious worship is to be given to God, the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost; and to him alone; not to angels, saints, or any other creature

positions.statement: The saints are remembered as examples of faith; no claim is made that they pray for us, and they are not to be addressed in prayer.
positions.mark: The passage says prayer is to be made to God alone and never to departed saints, without saying the saints pray for us.
positions.first_defined: Westminster Confession, 21.2 (1646)

positions.name: The saints pray for the Church, but are not to be invoked

defined.source: Apology of the Augsburg Confession, XXI.9 (1531)
defined.quote: concerning the saints we concede that, just as, when alive, they pray for the Church universal in general, so in heaven they pray for the Church in general
But the Scripture teaches not the invocation of saints or to ask help of saints, since it sets before us the one Christ as the Mediator

positions.statement: The saints in heaven pray for the Church in general, but Christians should not call on them or ask their help.
positions.mark: The passage says departed saints pray for the Church while denying that Christians should address them.
positions.first_defined: Augsburg Confession XXI (1530); Apology XXI (1531)

positions.name: Asking the saints to pray for us

defined.source: Council of Trent, Session 25, On the invocation of saints (1563)
defined.quote: the saints, who reign together with Christ, offer up their own prayers to God for men; that it is good and useful suppliantly to invoke them

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 8 (1672)
defined.quote: Notwithstanding, in [our] prayers and supplications unto Him, we say the Saints are intercessors, and, above all, the undefiled Mother of the very God the Word

positions.statement: Departed saints pray for the living, and it is right to address them directly and ask for their prayers.
positions.mark: The passage addresses a departed saint directly (such as 'pray for us') or teaches that Christians should ask departed saints for their prayers.
positions.first_defined: Council of Trent, Session 25 (1563); Synod of Jerusalem (1672)

first_states.author: Asterius of Amasea
first_states.text: Thus a father or mother, taking up a sick child and embracing it, runs to seek medicine and doctors, but turns to unskilled help; and coming to one of the martyrs, she presents her petition to the Lord with the same cries used toward the Mediator: 'Intercede through Christ's suffering for those who suffer and are sick. With boldness, use your voice for fellow-servants. Even if you left our life behind, you know the sufferings of humanity; you yourself once pleaded before becoming a martyr. When you sought, you received; now having received, grant. Ask for your own benefit in the form of old age. May we be healed of our infirmity as the world is healed by Christ.'

commemoration-only.quote: coming to one of the martyrs, she presents her petition to the Lord with the same cries used toward the Mediator: 'Intercede through Christ's suffering for those who suffer and are sick.'
commemoration-only.audited: The mother addresses the martyr: 'Having suffered for Christ, intercede (πρέσβευσον) for suffering and disease', a direct request to a departed saint, presented approvingly by Asterius.

pray-but-not-invoked.quote: coming to one of the martyrs, she presents her petition to the Lord with the same cries used toward the Mediator: 'Intercede through Christ's suffering... With boldness, use your voice for fellow-servants.'
pray-but-not-invoked.audited: A departed martyr is directly asked: 'πρέσβευσον... χρῆσον λόγον τοῖς ὁμοδούλοις' ('intercede... speak for your fellow servants').

invocation.quote: coming to one of the martyrs, she presents her petition to the Lord with the same cries used toward the Mediator: 'Intercede through Christ's suffering for those who suffer and are sick. With boldness, use your voice for fellow-servants.'
invocation.audited: Direct address to a martyr: 'Παθὼν διὰ Χριστὸν πρέσβευσον ὑπὲρ πάθους καὶ νόσου' ('you who suffered for Christ, intercede for suffering and sickness'). The English 'Intercede through Christ's suffering' and 'the same cries used toward the Mediator' mistranslate: the Greek calls the martyr the go-between (πρὸς τὸν μεσίτην).

passages.author: Amphilochius of Iconium
passages.text: In that [passage]: 'Father, if it is possible.' The discourse of our holy father Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, against the heretics, concerning: 'Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me' (Matt 26:39). Again, like a lawful soldier, I take up the fight against the heretics, with Stephen, the commander of piety, leading the ranks. For just as Jesus was turning the enemies when Moses was praying, so also I, with the martyr cooperating, lay hold of the enemies of the truth. I say these things not daring through an abundance of words, but having trusted in the prayer of the martyr, I dare to speak these words. For I do not fear their bulk in words. I fear the obstacles of their bad-crafty deception. For we learned not to fear a fear that did not exist.

commemoration-only.quote: having trusted in the prayer of the martyr, I dare to speak these words
commemoration-only.audited: 'Having trusted in the prayer of the martyr (τῇ προσευχῇ τοῦ μάρτυρος πεποιθώς)' Stephen, with 'the martyr cooperating', says a departed saint prays for the living speaker.

passages.author: Asterius of Amasea
passages.text: Thus a father or mother, taking up a sick child and embracing it, runs to seek medicine and doctors, but turns to unskilled help; and coming to one of the martyrs, she presents her petition to the Lord with the same cries used toward the Mediator: 'Intercede through Christ's suffering for those who suffer and are sick. With boldness, use your voice for fellow-servants. Even if you left our life behind, you know the sufferings of humanity; you yourself once pleaded before becoming a martyr. When you sought, you received; now having received, grant. Ask for your own benefit in the form of old age. May we be healed of our infirmity as the world is healed by Christ.'

commemoration-only.audited: The mother addresses the martyr: 'Having suffered for Christ, intercede (πρέσβευσον) for suffering and disease', a direct request to a departed saint, presented approvingly by Asterius.

pray-but-not-invoked.quote: coming to one of the martyrs, she presents her petition to the Lord with the same cries used toward the Mediator: 'Intercede through Christ's suffering... With boldness, use your voice for fellow-servants.'
pray-but-not-invoked.audited: A departed martyr is directly asked: 'πρέσβευσον... χρῆσον λόγον τοῖς ὁμοδούλοις' ('intercede... speak for your fellow servants').

invocation.quote: coming to one of the martyrs, she presents her petition to the Lord with the same cries used toward the Mediator: 'Intercede through Christ's suffering for those who suffer and are sick. With boldness, use your voice for fellow-servants.'
invocation.audited: Direct address to a martyr: 'Παθὼν διὰ Χριστὸν πρέσβευσον ὑπὲρ πάθους καὶ νόσου' ('you who suffered for Christ, intercede for suffering and sickness'). The English 'Intercede through Christ's suffering' and 'the same cries used toward the Mediator' mistranslate: the Greek calls the martyr the go-between (πρὸς τὸν μεσίτην).

passages.author: Asterius of Amasea
passages.text: For our prayer is not sufficient to move God in the time of necessity or misfortune, for our plea is not a persuasion, but a remembrance of sins; therefore we fly to the fellow-servants who are loved by the Lord, so that they might heal our defects through their own achievements. What then is the charge, that while honoring martyrs we ourselves strive to please God? What accusation is there in flying to protectors? Let us examine also these things, if the accuser cleanses the charge. And how [can it be said], that you do not honor myriads of dead men, but worship them as gods?

commemoration-only.quote: we fly to the fellow-servants who are loved by the Lord, so that they might heal our defects through their own achievements
commemoration-only.audited: 'We flee to the fellow-servants loved by the Lord, so that they might heal our faults by their own achievements' and 'we enjoy their patronage before God' (Greek προσφεύγομεν, προστασίας... πρὸς Θεόν) is seeking help from departed martyrs.

passages.author: Asterius of Amasea
passages.text: The martyrs are not respected even for the greatness of the miracles. Instead, people call them many-maned, and their tombs and their resting places are named as such, and they cleanse themselves as if rubbing against a contagion, not even mentioning that God-breathed saying praised by every mouth: 'Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His saints' (Psalm 116:15). Therefore, let us pray to God, and let us entreat the martyrs to revile the Lord in common, so that a spirit of compunction may be given to those acting under the error of heresy, and the division may be loosed like a mediator or a barrier, so that all may come together in brotherly unity in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belongs the glory forever. Amen.

commemoration-only.quote: let us entreat the martyrs to revile the Lord in common
commemoration-only.audited: 'Let us entreat the martyrs (παρακαλέσωμεν δὲ μάρτυρας) to implore our common Master' asks departed martyrs to pray.

pray-but-not-invoked.quote: let us entreat the martyrs to revile the Lord in common
pray-but-not-invoked.audited: Christians are told to 'entreat the martyrs' (παρακαλέσωμεν δὲ μάρτυρας), the request this position forbids.

invocation.quote: let us entreat the martyrs to revile the Lord in common
invocation.audited: 'Let us pray to God, and let us entreat the martyrs to implore our common Master' (παρακαλέσωμεν δὲ μάρτυρας τὸν κοινὸν δυσωπῆσαι Δεσπότην) teaches asking the martyrs for prayer. The English 'revile the Lord in common' is a serious mistranslation of δυσωπῆσαι ('implore').

passages.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
passages.text: It should be believed that he is truly the holy Longinus, the centurion who confessed Christ on the cross, by whose intercession and consolation we are all preserved, both those who read and those who hear, in Christ.

commemoration-only.quote: by whose intercession and consolation we are all preserved
commemoration-only.audited: 'Holy Longinus... by whose intercession (πρεσβείᾳ) we are all preserved' says a departed saint intercedes for the living. The Greek is a wish ('may we be preserved', διαφυλαχθείημεν).

questions.question: Is Scripture the only infallible rule of faith, or is Church tradition also binding?
shared_ground: Scripture is inspired by God and true
Scripture is sufficient to refute heretics or to teach the faith (praise of Scripture alone decides nothing)
Heretics misinterpret Scripture
The 'rule of faith' or creed summarizes apostolic teaching
Church teachers and councils are to be respected

positions.name: Scripture the only infallible rule

defined.source: Formula of Concord, Epitome, Rule and Norm, 1 (1577)
defined.quote: the sole rule and standard according to which all dogmas together with [all] teachers should be estimated and judged are the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures of the Old and of the New Testament alone

The supreme judge by which all controversies of religion are to be determined, and all decrees of councils, opinions of ancient writers, doctrines of men, and private spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture.

Holy Scripture containeth all things necessary to salvation: so that whatsoever is not read therein, nor may be proved thereby, is not to be required of any man, that it should be believed as an article of the Faith

positions.statement: Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith; councils, fathers and traditions are judged by it, and nothing not provable from it may be required as necessary belief.
positions.mark: The passage says nothing may be believed as necessary unless proved from Scripture, or that councils and church teachers are to be judged by Scripture as the final norm.
positions.first_defined: Formula of Concord (1577); Thirty-Nine Articles (1563/1571); Westminster Confession (1646)

positions.name: Scripture with binding Church tradition

defined.quote: receives and venerates with an equal affection of piety, and reverence, all the books both of the Old and of the New Testament ... as also the said traditions, as well those appertaining to faith as to morals

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 2 (1672)
defined.quote: the witness also of the Catholic Church is, we believe, not of inferior authority to that of the Divine Scriptures.

positions.statement: Unwritten apostolic tradition, kept in the Church, binds with the same authority as Scripture, and the Church's interpretation of Scripture is authoritative.
positions.mark: The passage says some practice or doctrine is held from unwritten apostolic tradition with binding force, or that the Church's tradition holds equal authority with Scripture.
positions.first_defined: Council of Trent, Session 4 (1546); Synod of Jerusalem, Decree 2 (1672)

questions.question: Which books belong to the Old Testament?
shared_ground: The books of the Hebrew canon are Scripture (all positions)
The 27 books of the New Testament are Scripture (all positions)
Quoting Wisdom or Sirach as wise or edifying without calling it Scripture

positions.name: Hebrew canon only

defined.quote: The books commonly called Apocrypha, not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of the Scripture

positions.statement: The Old Testament consists only of the books of the Hebrew canon; the others are not inspired.
positions.mark: The passage limits the Old Testament to the Hebrew books (such as a count of 22 or 24 books) and puts Wisdom, Sirach, Tobit, Judith and Maccabees outside Scripture.
positions.first_defined: Westminster Confession (1646)

positions.name: Read for example of life, not for doctrine

defined.quote: And the other Books (as Hierome saith) the Church doth read for example of life and instruction of manners; but yet doth it not apply them to establish any doctrine

positions.statement: The extra books are read in church for example and instruction, but are not used to establish doctrine.
positions.mark: The passage says these books are read in church or to learners but are not used to prove doctrine.
positions.first_defined: Thirty-Nine Articles, Article VI (1563/1571)

positions.name: Wider canon as full Scripture

defined.quote: Tobias, Judith, Esther, Job, the Davidical Psalter, consisting of a hundred and fifty psalms; the Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Canticle of Canticles, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Question 3 (1672)
defined.quote: For we judge these also to be with the other genuine Books of Divine Scripture genuine parts of Scripture.

positions.statement: Books such as Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and Maccabees are inspired Scripture on the same footing as the rest.
positions.mark: The passage lists these books among the canonical Scriptures, or cites them with full scriptural authority to prove doctrine.
positions.first_defined: Councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397), local; Council of Trent (1546); Synod of Jerusalem (1672)

passages.author: Origen of Alexandria
passages.text: You objected that I used Susanna as if unaware some call it uncanonical. I answer from the wider fact: in many holy books we find more or less than the Hebrews transmit — in Job and elsewhere verses stand with us that are absent there, and the church’s edification has long received these books. Still I do not refuse to search the Jewish copies; I refuse to move the ancient landmarks set for the churches.

hebrew-canon.quote: the church's edification has long received these books
hebrew-canon.audited: Kept. Origen defends having used 'the Scripture of Daniel concerning Susanna' (Greek συνεχρώμην τῇ ... Γραφῇ), a section 'carried in every Church of Christ' though absent from the Hebrew, and refuses to move the churches' landmarks, so he counts Susanna as Scripture. questions.question: On what basis is a sinner justified before God?
