first_uncertain.author: Severianus of Gabala
first_uncertain.text: The Savior, having received this voice, says: 'Today salvation has come to this house' (Luke 19:9). He justified himself, not because he simply saw Christ, but because he obeyed the laws of Christ. Today salvation has come to this house, because this man also is a son of Abraham. Before doing the works of Abraham, he does not call him a son of Abraham, but calls him Zacchaeus by the bare appellation; but when he fulfilled the works of the patriarch, promising charity and the restitution of the injustice, then he says: 'And this man also is a son of Abraham.'

forensic-imputation.quote: He justified himself, not because he simply saw Christ, but because he obeyed the laws of Christ
forensic-imputation.audited: 'He justified himself, not because he simply saw Christ, but because he obeyed the laws of Christ' (Αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν ἐδικαίωσεν... ἐπειδὴ τοῖς Χριστοῦ ὑπήκουσε νόμοις); salvation comes when he 'fulfilled the works of the patriarch'. Greek checked: faithful. Justification by obedience rules out faith-alone imputation. Borderline: homiletic, playing on his self-condemnation just before.

infused-righteousness.quote: He justified himself, not because he simply saw Christ, but because he obeyed the laws of Christ
infused-righteousness.audited: Zacchaeus is justified 'because he obeyed the laws of Christ', and the sermon continues 'let us adorn faith with works' (σεμνύνωμεν τοῖς ἔργοις τὴν πίστιν). That is justification by faith together with works. Borderline: a preacher's point, not a definition. passages.author: Origen of Alexandria
passages.text: And blessed is the one who has a part in the first resurrection, who has kept the baptism of the Holy Spirit. Who is the one saved in another resurrection? Therefore, these things being said, gathering as far as we can the words of the Scriptures, let us store them in the heart and try to live according to them, if perhaps we may be able to become clean before the departure, and, having prepared our works for the departure, going out may be taken up in those good things and be saved in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the power to the ages of the ages. passages.text: Fire was kindled. Let us use that song of Miriam the sister of Moses, for it is fitting for us now just as it was for them then. shared_ground: God the Father, in his divine nature, cannot be pictured
Worship (latria) belongs to God alone
Idols of pagan gods are forbidden
The Incarnation made God visible in Christ (shared doctrine; not by itself an argument for icons)

positions.name: Images venerated

defined.quote: the honour paid to an image traverses it, reaching the model, and he who venerates the image, venerates the person represented in that image.

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Question 4 (1672)
defined.quote: the honor paid to the Icon is not at all divided or at all different from [the honor paid to the one who] is portrayed

positions.statement: Images of Christ, Mary and the saints should be set up and honoured with outward signs (kissing, bowing, lights, incense); the honour passes to the person shown and differs from the worship due to God.
positions.mark: The passage approves honouring an image with outward acts (kissing, bowing, lights, incense), or says honour given to an image passes to the person shown.
positions.first_defined: Second Council of Nicaea (787)

positions.name: Images allowed as adornment, not venerated

defined.source: Apology of the Augsburg Confession, XXIV.51 (1531)
defined.quote: Candles, golden vessels [tapers, altar-cloths, images), and similar adornments are becoming, but they are not the adornment that properly belongs to the Church.

positions.statement: Images may be kept in churches as adornment or for teaching, but no honour is to be paid to them.
positions.mark: The passage allows images in churches for decoration or teaching while forbidding any honour or reverence toward them.
positions.first_defined: Apology of the Augsburg Confession (1531)

positions.name: Images not to be used in worship

defined.quote: But may not images be permitted in churches in place of books for the unlearned? A. No, we should not try to be wiser than God.
under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the Holy Scripture

positions.statement: Images have no place in churches or in worship; God is to be taught by the preached Word, not by pictures.
positions.mark: The passage says images must not be in churches or used in worship at all, not only that they must not be honoured.
positions.first_defined: Heidelberg Catechism (1563); Westminster Confession (1646)

first_uncertain.author: Epiphanius of Salamis
first_uncertain.text: He presents a testament to the citizens, a binding testament, in which he urges them not to bring images into churches or into the cemeteries. "Pay attention to yourselves and hold fast the traditions you received. Do not turn aside to the right or to the left. And in this matter, beloved children, keep memory: do not bring images into churches or into the cemeteries of the saints. Instead, always keep God in memory in your hearts. But not even in an ordinary house is this permitted, for a Christian must not be distracted through the eyes and the wanderings of the mind. Let the things toward God be written and impressed on all. If anyone deliberately endeavors to depict the divine character of God's Word according to the incarnation from material colors, let him be anathema."

venerated.audited: Kept. 'Do not bring images into churches or into the cemeteries of the saints' (Greek μὴ ἀναφέρειν εἰκόνας ἐπ' ἐκκλησίας) forbids images in churches. questions.question: On what basis does God predestine people to salvation, and is anyone predestined to condemnation?
shared_ground: God foreknows all things
Salvation is by God's grace, not earned
God is not the author of sin
Romans 8:29-30 and Ephesians 1 quoted on predestination without stating its basis
Some are saved and some are lost

positions.name: Election to life only

defined.quote: The predestination or eternal election of God, however, extends only over the godly, beloved children of God, being a cause of their salvation

positions.statement: God's election by grace is the cause of the salvation of the elect; there is no corresponding decree of reprobation, and the lost perish by their own fault.
positions.mark: The passage says God's predestination is only to salvation and that those who perish are not passed over or ordained to it by God's decree.
positions.first_defined: Formula of Concord, Article XI (1577)

positions.name: Election and reprobation (double predestination)

defined.quote: By the decree of God, for the manifestation of his glory, some men and angels are predestinated unto everlasting life; and others foreordained to everlasting death.

defined.source: Canons of Dort, First Head, Article 15 (1619)
defined.quote: not all people have been chosen but that some have not been chosen or have been passed by in God's eternal election

positions.statement: By an unconditional decree God chose some for life and passed by the rest, leaving them to just condemnation for their sins.
positions.mark: The passage says God chose some and passed by or rejected others by his own decree, not because of foreseen merit or faith.
positions.first_defined: Synod of Dort (1619); Westminster Confession (1646)

positions.name: Predestination according to foreseen free choice

defined.source: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem), Decree 3 (1672)
defined.quote: But since He foreknew the one would make a right use of their free-will, and the other a wrong, He predestinated the one, or condemned the other.

positions.statement: God predestines to glory those he foreknows will freely cooperate with his grace, and condemns those he foreknows will refuse it.
positions.mark: The passage says God predestines or chooses people because he foresees their faith, works or free response.
positions.first_defined: Synod of Jerusalem, Decree 3 (1672)

first_states.author: Origen of Alexandria
first_states.text: We must not confuse the order of divine action: it is not that God first predestines and then calls, but that His foreknowledge precedes and undergirds both. The psalm’s words about sinners alienated from the womb are not to be read as a denial of human responsibility, but as a description of a condition that, from birth, inclines toward falsehood—yet even then, the capacity for choice remains, however dim. To imagine that infants could speak lies in unison at birth is to misunderstand both language and moral agency. But when we read Paul’s own words in Galatians, we see that his separation from the womb was not a mere natural endowment, but a divine act aimed at revealing Christ in him—thus grounding the apostolic calling in God’s purpose, not human merit. This is why we affirm that all things work together for good for those who love God, not because they earned it, but because they we

double.quote: If we reverse this order and make predestination the first cause, we open the door to those who would blame God for injustice, as if He arbitrarily chose some and rejected others.
double.audited: Predestination is placed under foreknowledge of 'hearts inclined toward virtue', which grounds it in something foreseen in the person. Greek check: the English is a loose paraphrase; 'as if He arbitrarily chose some and rejected others' is not in the Greek, which targets those who bring in people 'saved by constitution and nature' (ἐκ κατασκευῆς καὶ φύσεως σωζομένους). The exclusion holds on the Greek of the following lines, not on that sentence.

foreknowledge.quote: God's foreknowledge is not the cause of what comes to be, but the reflection of His knowledge of what will be, grounded in His eternal understanding of hearts inclined toward virtue or alienation.
foreknowledge.audited: 'Foreknowledge precedes and undergirds' predestination, grounded in God's knowledge of 'hearts inclined toward virtue'. The Greek supports this (ἀνωτέρω δέ ἐστι τοῦ προορισμοῦ ἡ πρόγνωσις), but this English is an inflated paraphrase; cite b261abd049f379f3 for the exact words.

passages.author: Origen (catena heading)
passages.text: 9 Originating from the interpretation into 'according to the foreknowledge of God.' For God, having foreseen the faith and the works of men having been perfected in them through the evangelical teaching, foreknowingly chose them in Christ before the foundation of the world, having then predestined them to be sons through the participation of the spirit of sonship; for foreknowledge is to be regarded as nothing other than a vision of things to come, which is no longer foreknowledge, but is knowledge toward the existence of those having been foreseen; even so, according to foreknowledge, they were chosen, as Peter writes (1 Pet 1:2), but not now is the favor being made to them; thus he casts aside the myth concerning natures and the thought contained within.

double.quote: God, having foreseen the faith and the works of men having been perfected in them through the evangelical teaching, foreknowingly chose them
double.audited: Election rests on foreseen faith and conduct: 'having foreseen the faith and conduct (Προεωρακὼς... τὴν πίστιν καὶ πρᾶξιν)... he chose them'. That rules out a choice made without regard to anything foreseen.

foreknowledge.audited: 'Having foreseen the faith and conduct of men... he chose them in Christ before the foundation of the world, then predestining them' (Προεωρακὼς γὰρ ὁ θεὸς τὴν πίστιν καὶ πρᾶξιν... ἐξελέξατο αὐτούς... προορίσας). Therefore, let us follow the sequence of what has been said: God justifies because He called beforehand; He would not justify those He did not call; and He calls because He predestined beforehand; He would not call those He did not predestine; and it is to Him that the beginning of the call and justification belongs, not predestination. For if predestination were the starting point of what follows, those who advance the strange argument of nature would easily prevail. But above predestination lies foreknowledge: for whom He foreknew, He declares, He also predestined to be conformed to the image

double.quote: having considered the inclination of these things in us toward security and impulse after that inclination, and as they will surrender themselves wholly to living according to virtue, He foreknew them

foreknowledge.audited: 'Having considered the inclination of what is in our power in certain people toward piety... and that they will give themselves wholly to living by virtue, He foreknew them... and whom He so foreknew, He predestined' (κατανοήσας ῥοπὴν τοῦ ἐφ' ἡμῖν τῶνδέ τινων ἐπὶ εὐσέβειαν... καὶ οὓς οὕτω προέγνω, προώρισεν). Greek checked (Philocalia 25 text, Romans catena). TRANSLATION: the English 'toward security' mistranslates εὐσέβειαν ('piety').

passages.author: Origen of Alexandria
passages.text: If someone insists these events could not have taken place, we respond that they might not have occurred, but it does not follow that if something is incapable of happening, it must either happen or fail to happen; events unfold not solely by necessity, but also as contingent possibilities, including the possibility of non-occurrence. The examination of what is possible engages both logical analysis and reflective insight, enabling one who turns inward to perceive the subtlety of arguments and grasp how even fortuitous occurrences do not obstruct the potential for something to be actual in multiple ways—one of many possibilities becoming real, not by compulsion. God foreknew that events would unfold not through necessity but as free possibilities, and the declaration that they would occur is not speculative guesswork but genuine foreknowledge. Let no one suppose we have remained silent o

double.quote: those whom he foreknew, he also predestined
double.audited: Origen says the cause of the purpose and of the foreknowledge lies in what is in our power, so election is not independent of the person. The grader's quote (bare Rom 8:29) did not support the verdict; the deciding words are given here.

foreknowledge.quote: those whom he foreknew, he also predestined
foreknowledge.audited: 'He makes clear that the cause of the purpose and of the foreknowledge comes from what is in our power' (τὴν ἐκ τοῦ ἐφ' ἡμῖν αἰτίαν παρίστησι τῆς προθέσεως καὶ τῆς προγνώσεως). The grader's quote, the bare 'those whom he foreknew, he also predestined', is shared ground; the verdict holds only on these words. Greek checked.

Moreover, even if one were set apart for the gospel of God from the womb and had necessity imposed upon them, how could they consistently speak of subduing their body and leading into slavery if they had not yet been declared unapproved by others, and the woe would be theirs if they did not evangelize? Clearly, from this it follows that if they had not subdued their body and led into slavery, it would have been possible for them to be declared unapproved by others, and it was possible for woe to befall them had they not evangelized. foreknowledge.audited: 'Perhaps (μήποτε) God set him apart from the womb... having seen the cause of the just setting-apart: that he would subdue his body' (σὺν τῷ ἑωρακέναι τὴν αἰτίαν τοῦ δικαίου ἀφορισμοῦ). Greek checked: faithful, including the hedge 'perhaps'. It concerns Paul's apostolic calling, not salvation as such; b261abd049f379f3 is the stronger witness.

passages.author: Diodorus of Tarsus
passages.text: Whom then did God glorify here? Those whom he justified. And whom did he predestine? Those whom he foreknew, those being called according to purpose, that is, those being worthy to be called and to be conformed to Christ through their own purpose. He brings forward the great proof of the love of God, having shown through his deeds that all things work together for our good through the love of God toward us, namely, those whom he found to be called according to purpose, which he demonstrated in not sparing the only-begotten (Rom 8:31–32); for what, if even death did not overpower the Savior, since even upon the Lord he cast down his soul and received it again? But nevertheless it must be observed that Christ subjected himself to sufferings for the sake of humans, fulfilling both his own and the will of the Father. Therefore, since God is managing all things for our sake, who will hinder?

double.quote: those being worthy to be called and to be conformed to Christ through their own purpose
double.audited: The predestined are 'those worthy to be called... through their own purpose', grounding the choice in the person's own purpose.

foreknowledge.quote: those being called according to purpose, that is, those being worthy to be called and to be conformed to Christ through their own purpose
foreknowledge.audited: 'Whom did he predestine? Those whom he foreknew... that is, those who are worthy to be called and conformed to Christ through their own purpose' (τοὺς διὰ τὴν ἰδίαν πρόθεσιν ἀξίους ὄντας κληθῆναι). Greek checked: faithful.

passages.attribution_note: A catena fragment: the ascription rests on the catena heading and is not secure.

passages.author: Didymus the Blind
passages.text: He might pass from one [state] to another. If he had not become one in the truth, not standing in it would not have brought him reproach. And behold the doctrine: how 'God wants all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth' (1 Tim 2:4)? If no one opposes His will, how is it that some are lagging behind, despite His wanting all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth—so that I may not say, the majority? If He wants [it], and if we also want [it], and a convergence of the two wills occurs, salvation happens; for no one is good against his will, no one who does not want is saved, and no one hurrying toward approaching God and having kept His law is able to know the truth.

double.quote: no one is good against his will, no one who does not want is saved
double.audited: 'God wants all men to be saved', and salvation needs 'a convergence of the two wills'. This fits the double position's own exclusion clause: he wills all to be saved.

passages.author: Didymus the Blind
passages.text: Again, concerning Esau and Jacob, the apostle, as if speaking in a dilemma, says: 'What then shall we say to this? Is there injustice with God? May it never be!' (Romans 9:14). Because he had refuted injustice, he forced us to seek how there is not injustice with God. If it were so, as those who speak of foreknowledge say, we would rather find injustice in Him. 'I loved Jacob,' He says, 'but I hated Esau' (Romans 9:13). But one is hated or loved according to things done and according to things thought. How then does foreknowledge have room? Is injustice found with God? But he, refuting this, said: 'What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? May it never be!' Since there is no injustice, let the matter be sought in another way, how it has come to pass.

foreknowledge.quote: If it were so, as those who speak of foreknowledge say, we would rather find injustice in Him
foreknowledge.audited: 'If it were as those who speak of foreknowledge say, we would rather find injustice with Him... How then does foreknowledge have room?' (πῶς οὖν χώραν ἔχει ἡ πρόγνωσις;). Greek checked: faithful. Didymus rejects foreknowledge as the basis and grounds love and hate in things actually done and thought. That is not an unconditional decree, so it gives no support to 'double'.

passages.author: Didymus the Blind
passages.text: But did Paul speak according to foreknowledge? Foreknowledge is a theoretical viewing of what is coming to be. But according to kind, foreknowledge and knowledge are the same. They differ in time. For example, suppose I foreknow that tomorrow there will be thunder. When the thunder comes to be in the middle of the day, it is knowledge, no longer foreknowledge. And the knowledge of the thunder does not make it such, but what it is, that becomes the knowledge. Thus the known thing makes the knowledge, which does not receive the knowing from us. I use an image for the sake of the manner of foreknowledge: the one [child] is born so that he may demand, and the other, so that he may live in the house. What kind of justice is this of foreknowledge, if we take these things to happen according to foreknowledge? Foreknowledge both justifies and condemns. To foreknow and to know is also to condemn
